---
title: "California Wildfire Analysis"
author: Ethan Anghelache
output: html_document
---

How much do human factors (population, WUI housing growth, roads) explain where wildfires start in California, and can they predict which counties face rising ignition risk?

```{r}
# Load Libraries
library(RSQLite)  # SQL for Fire Data
library(DBI)
library(sf)       # Spatial Data
library(dplyr)    # Data Wrangling
library(tmap)     # Mapping Visualizations
library(tigris)   # Defining our Region
library(randomForest)  # Machine Learning

options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)

# Load Data
ca_counties <- counties(state = "CA", cb = TRUE, progress_bar = FALSE)
ca_counties <- st_transform(ca_counties, st_crs(ca_wui))  # see note below

# Fire database (SQL)
con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), "data/RDS_SQL/FPA_FOD_20260615.sqlite")

# California WUI blocks (filtered from the national file once, in the Console)
ca_wui <- st_read("data/OtherData/ca_wui.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

# Preview the fire data (SQL)
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT FIRE_YEAR, DISCOVERY_DATE, NWCG_CAUSE_CLASSIFICATION,
         FIRE_SIZE, LATITUDE, LONGITUDE, FIPS_NAME
  FROM Fires
  WHERE STATE = 'CA'
  LIMIT 5
")

# Preview the WUI data (key columns only, without the shape data)
head(st_drop_geometry(ca_wui)[, c("BLK20", "fips", "HU2000", "HU2020",
                                  "WUIFLAG2000", "WUIFLAG2020", "VEG2019PC")])

# Preview the counties
head(st_drop_geometry(ca_counties)[, c("NAME", "GEOID", "ALAND")])
```

**Data overview (draft):** This project combines three sources. The FPA FOD fire database
records every reported wildfire in the U.S. from 1992–2024, including where it started, when,
how large it grew, and whether it was human- or lightning-caused; I query it with SQL and keep
only California fires. The SILVIS WUI dataset gives housing counts, wild land vegetation, and
WUI status for every census block in 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020, filtered to California's
[X] blocks. County boundaries from the U.S. Census (via `tigris`) tie everything together so
fires and housing can be compared county by county.

## 2. California fires over time

```{r}
fires_year <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT FIRE_YEAR, COUNT(*) AS n_fires
  FROM Fires
  WHERE STATE = 'CA'
  GROUP BY FIRE_YEAR
  ORDER BY FIRE_YEAR
")

plot(fires_year$FIRE_YEAR, fires_year$n_fires, type = "b",
     main = "California wildfire ignitions per year",
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Number of fires",
     pch = 21, bg = "dodgerblue", col = "black")
```

**Takeaway (draft):** California averages roughly 7,000–9,000 wildfire ignitions per year,
with no clear upward trend from 1992 to 2024. The biggest exception is 2005–2008, peaking at
about 13,400 fires in 2007, though part of this spike may reflect changes in how agencies
reported fires. Since fires have grown more destructive while the number of ignitions has
stayed fairly flat, the more useful question we try to answer is not how many fires start, but where they
start and who starts them.

## 3. Is it us? Human vs. lightning ignitions

```{r}
cause_year <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT FIRE_YEAR, NWCG_CAUSE_CLASSIFICATION AS cause, COUNT(*) AS n_fires
  FROM Fires
  WHERE STATE = 'CA'
  GROUP BY FIRE_YEAR, cause
")

human   <- cause_year[cause_year$cause == "Human", ]
natural <- cause_year[cause_year$cause == "Natural", ]
unknown <- cause_year[cause_year$cause == "Missing data/not specified/undetermined", ]

plot(human$FIRE_YEAR, human$n_fires, type = "b",
     ylim = c(0, max(cause_year$n_fires)),
     main = "California wildfire ignitions by cause",
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Number of fires",
     pch = 21, bg = "red", col = "black")
lines(natural$FIRE_YEAR, natural$n_fires, type = "b",
      pch = 21, bg = "dodgerblue", col = "black")
lines(unknown$FIRE_YEAR, unknown$n_fires, type = "b",
      pch = 21, bg = "gray70", col = "black")
legend("topright", legend = c("Human", "Lightning", "Unknown"),
       pt.bg = c("red", "dodgerblue", "gray70"), pch = 21)
```

**Takeaway (draft):** Among fires with a known cause, humans start the large majority of
California's wildfires. Human ignitions outnumber lightning ignitions every year from 1992 to
2021, and in 2020, 88.7% of known-cause fires were human-caused. However, the share of fires
with an unknown cause has grown from about 21% in 2015 to 45% in 2020, and above 78% after
2021, likely because many recent cause investigations are incomplete. The apparent decline in
human-caused fires is therefore uncertain, so this project limits cause-based analysis to
2000–2020 and uses total ignitions for modeling.
## 4. Ignition density by county

```{r}
# Pull California fires from 2000–2020 (SQL)
ca_fires <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT FIRE_YEAR, NWCG_CAUSE_CLASSIFICATION AS cause,
         FIRE_SIZE, LATITUDE, LONGITUDE
  FROM Fires
  WHERE STATE = 'CA'
    AND FIRE_YEAR BETWEEN 2000 AND 2020
")

# Turn coordinates into map points, then match each fire to its county
fires_sf <- st_as_sf(ca_fires, coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"), crs = 4269)
fires_sf <- st_transform(fires_sf, st_crs(ca_counties))
fires_sf <- st_join(fires_sf, ca_counties[, c("GEOID", "NAME")])

nrow(fires_sf)
```

```{r}
county_fires <- fires_sf |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(GEOID)) |>              # drop any points that fell offshore
  group_by(GEOID) |>
  summarise(n_total   = n(),
            n_human   = sum(cause == "Human"),
            n_natural = sum(cause == "Natural"))

# Join counts to county shapes and calculate fires per 100 km² per year
n_years <- 21  # 2000–2020

ca_counties <- ca_counties |>
  left_join(county_fires, by = "GEOID") |>
  mutate(area_km2        = ALAND / 1e6,
         human_density   = round(n_human   / area_km2 * 100 / n_years, 3),
         natural_density = round(n_natural / area_km2 * 100 / n_years, 3),
         human_share     = round(n_human / n_total, 3))
```

```{r}
ca_counties |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(human_density)) |>
  select(NAME, n_human, n_natural, human_density, natural_density, human_share) |>
  head(10)
```

```{r}
tm_shape(ca_counties) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("human_density", "natural_density"),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                              values = "brewer.or_rd"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Fires per 100 km² per year")) +
  tm_layout(panel.labels = c("Human-caused", "Lightning-caused"))
```

**Takeaway (draft):** From 2000–2020, 184,585 California wildfires were matched to counties.
The highest human-caused ignition densities are in the Bay Area (San Francisco, Santa Cruz,
Contra Costa) and Sierra Nevada foothill counties such as El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, and
Butte, which are areas where homes spread into dry, wooded land. Lightning fires show almost
the opposite pattern, concentrating in remote northern and high Sierra counties. Human
ignition densities also run far higher, reaching 7.207 fires per 100 km² per year compared to
a maximum of 1.499 for lightning. San Francisco's top ranking should be read with caution,
since its small area means relatively few fires (183) produce a high density.

## 5. WUI housing growth by county
```{r}
# Total WUI housing per county, 2000 vs. 2020
county_wui <- ca_wui |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(GEOID = substr(BLK20, 1, 5)) |>
  group_by(GEOID) |>
  summarise(wui_hu_2000 = sum(HU2000[WUIFLAG2000 > 0], na.rm = TRUE),
            wui_hu_2020 = sum(HU2020[WUIFLAG2020 > 0], na.rm = TRUE),
            veg_pct     = mean(VEG2019PC, na.rm = TRUE))

head(county_wui)
```

```{r}
#Growth and join to counties
ca_counties <- ca_counties |>
  left_join(county_wui, by = "GEOID") |>
  mutate(wui_growth_pct = round((wui_hu_2020 - wui_hu_2000) / wui_hu_2000 * 100, 3),
         wui_new_units  = wui_hu_2020 - wui_hu_2000)

ca_counties |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(wui_growth_pct)) |>
  select(NAME, wui_hu_2000, wui_hu_2020, wui_new_units, wui_growth_pct) |>
  head(10)
```

```{r}
#Map it
tm_shape(ca_counties) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "wui_growth_pct",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                              values = "brewer.purples"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "WUI housing growth (%), 2000–2020"))


```
